name: TPO antibodies (thyroid peroxidase antibodies)
summary: Autoantibodies against thyroid peroxidase, an enzyme needed to make thyroid hormone; a positive result indicates autoimmune thyroid disease, usually Hashimoto's thyroiditis.
why_it_matters: TPO antibodies identify the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient countries and help predict who with a mildly raised TSH will progress to overt hypothyroidism. Positivity is common (about one in ten adults, more in women), and many positive people keep normal thyroid function for years, so a positive result is a risk marker, not a diagnosis.

ref_range.source: Roche Elecsys anti-TPO cutoff (<34 IU/mL); other platforms use different cutoffs, e.g. <9 or <35
ref_range.note: Cutoffs are assay-specific; results are best read as negative or positive. IU/mL = kIU/L.

deep:
## What it is

Thyroid peroxidase is the enzyme that iodinates thyroglobulin to make T4 and T3. Antibodies against it reflect autoimmune attack on the thyroid. They are found in about 90% of people with Hashimoto's thyroiditis and in most people with Graves' disease, as well as in some people with normal thyroid function. The level marks autoimmunity; it does not measure how well the thyroid is working.

## Why it matters

- **Prevalence.** In NHANES III about 11% of the US population was TPO-antibody positive, more often women and older adults and less often Black Americans (Hollowell 2002).
- **Progression risk.** In the 20-year Whickham follow-up (Vanderpump 1995), women with positive thyroid antibodies alone developed overt hypothyroidism at about 2% per year, those with raised TSH alone about 3% per year, and those with both about 4% per year.
- **Pregnancy.** Positivity is associated with miscarriage, preterm birth and postpartum thyroiditis, but the TABLET trial (Dhillon-Smith 2019) found levothyroxine did not improve live births in euthyroid TPO-positive women.

## How to read it

Units: IU/mL (equivalent to kIU/L). The positivity cutoff is **assay-specific** (for example under about 9, 34 or 35 IU/mL), and numbers from different labs are not interchangeable. Read the result as negative or positive and roughly how far above the cutoff; higher titers generally carry higher risk. No sex-specific range; women are simply positive more often. Population distributions (NHANES 2007-2012) are heavily right-skewed, so whether you are above the cutoff matters more than your percentile. There is no "optimal" level.

## Causes of high

Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves' disease, postpartum thyroiditis, other autoimmune diseases (type 1 diabetes, celiac disease, vitiligo, pernicious anemia), Down and Turner syndromes, high iodine intake at the population level, and drugs that trigger thyroid autoimmunity (immune checkpoint inhibitors, interferon-alpha, amiodarone, alemtuzumab).

## Causes of low

A negative result is the norm. Titers fall during pregnancy and may decline slowly over years or after thyroidectomy or radioiodine; a minority of people with Hashimoto's are antibody-negative.

## What moves it

- **Age and sex:** positivity rises with age and is several times more common in women.
- **Pregnancy:** titers usually fall and can rebound postpartum.
- **Selenium:** some trials found selenium lowers titers, but evidence that this improves outcomes is weak and inconsistent (Cochrane review, van Zuuren 2013).
- **Treatment:** levothyroxine treats the hormone deficit but does not reliably clear antibodies. Titers are fairly stable, so repeat testing is rarely informative.
- **Assay:** biotin can interfere with some TPO immunoassays.

## What to test alongside

TSH and free T4 (current thyroid function), thyroglobulin antibodies (another autoimmune marker that also interferes with thyroglobulin measurement), TSH-receptor antibodies for Graves', and thyroid ultrasound when clinically indicated.
